title: Embeddings: meaning as geometry
story:
Comparing two pieces of text by their characters fails at the first paraphrase. The strings differ and the meaning does not, and no amount of careful string handling closes that gap, because the information you need is not in the characters.

An embedding gives every item a position in a shared space, learned so that items appearing in similar contexts land near each other. After that, one operation does all the work: measure the distance. Relatedness, which was a question about meaning, becomes a question about coordinates, and coordinates are something a machine is fast at.

That is a genuine change in what is buildable, and nearly everything that retrieves by meaning rests on it. Notice what it rests on, though, because the rest of this lesson is about that. The space is produced by a training objective, and the objective was about which items occur near which other items. Distance in the space measures what the training made nearby. It does not measure truth, and it does not measure relevance to your question, except in so far as those things happen to correlate with co-occurrence in the data the model saw.

The demonstration everyone remembers comes from the 2013 paper by Mikolov, Chen, Corrado and Dean, which reports that the vector for king, minus the vector for man, plus the vector for woman, gives a vector closest to the representation of the word queen. It is a striking result: the geometry appears to hold a relation, not just a similarity, and the relation can be moved from one pair of words to another by arithmetic. The paper also introduced a test set of syntactic and semantic regularities to measure this properly, with thousands of questions in each category, rather than resting on the single famous example.

There is a detail in how that question is asked, and it changes what the answer means.

The implementations do not allow the input terms of the query to be returned as the answer. Nissim, van Noord and van der Goot documented this in 2020, in the default implementation of word2vec, in gensim, and in the code from Bolukbasi and colleagues from 2016. They adapted all three to allow the input words back into the candidate set, ran the original test set again, and macro-accuracy fell from 0.71 to 0.21 for the standard method, and from 0.73 to 0.45 for a variant of it. In most cases the reason is that the second term of the query is returned as the answer, which happens when no close neighbour is found — man is to king as woman is to king.

Sit with that particular failure, because it is not a small technical wrinkle. The nearest point to the computed vector is very often one of the words you started from. The arithmetic moved you a little, and the honest nearest neighbour to where you landed was still king. What made the answer come out as queen was partly the geometry and partly a rule saying king was not allowed to win.

Two things are worth getting right about this. The first is what it does not show. It does not show the space is empty of structure, and it does not make embeddings a trick — the same drop had been observed before, by Linzen in 2016 and Schluter in 2018, and the field kept using embeddings for good reason, because they work. The second is what it does show, which is that the relations are far weaker and far noisier than the demonstration implied, and the demonstration was doing part of its persuading through an exclusion rule that nobody quoting it mentioned. The authors say the constraint is mentioned in the original paper and in later work, and that they nonetheless believe it is not common knowledge in the field, where the analogy examples are still widely used.

The general form of the mistake outlives word vectors, which is why this belongs in your habits and not in your trivia. When a result depends on filtering the candidate answers, the filter is part of the result and has to be quoted with it. A retrieval system evaluated after removing the documents it would obviously have returned, a model scored on a test set with the confusing cases dropped, a benchmark where the trivial answer is excluded by construction — in every case the number describes the system and the filter together, and reporting only the number is reporting a different system from the one you have.

What survives the correction is the useful part, and it is most of the engineering. Meaning as geometry is how search over your own documents works, how duplicate detection works, how a recommendation finds a neighbour. Distance is a proxy for relatedness, it is a good one, and it is only ever as good as the objective that built the space. Treat it as an instrument with a known bias rather than as a window onto meaning, and it will do a great deal of work for you.

problem.name: Comparison by position in a learned space
problem.shape: Items must be compared by meaning, and their surface forms do not line up.
tell: the same thing is said in different words and must still match
exact matching returns nothing while a human sees an obvious hit
the set of possible categories is too large or too fluid to enumerate
you need a ranking rather than a yes or no
a demonstration of the geometry depends on which candidates were allowed to win
problem.move: Put every item into one space produced by one model, then compare by distance. Before trusting a result, state what the objective made nearby and check the candidate set: anything excluded from winning is part of the claim.
problem.invariant: Distances are only meaningful within a single space produced by a single model, because the coordinates have no meaning of their own — vectors from two models, or two versions of one model, are not comparable.
problem.breaks: Distance measures co-occurrence rather than truth or relevance, so statements that contradict each other sit close together. And any result that required excluding candidates from the answer set describes the space and the filter together.

cost.time: comparing a query against every item is linear in the number of items, which is what approximate indexes exist to avoid
cost.space: every item carries a vector of fixed width, so storage grows with the number of items and the width
cost.beats: exact matching, which cannot see a paraphrase, and a hand-built taxonomy, which covers only what somebody thought to enter

worked.problem: What is a vector distance actually measuring, and what did the analogy demonstration exclude?
worked.reasoning:
It measures what the training objective made nearby, which is co-occurrence in the data the model saw.

That is the whole of it, and keeping it in mind saves several bad decisions. The space was built so that items appearing in similar contexts land near each other. So a small distance is evidence of similar usage, and it is not evidence of truth, of relevance to my particular query, or of any relation I have not checked. Two statements that contradict each other appear in near-identical contexts and sit close together, which is exactly the case where a distance misleads you.

On the analogy demonstration, the thing to know is what the implementations exclude. The 2013 paper reports that the vector for king, minus man, plus woman, is closest to queen, and it introduced a proper test set of syntactic and semantic regularities rather than resting on that one example.

But the standard implementations do not allow the input terms of the query to be returned. Nissim, van Noord and van der Goot adapted the word2vec implementation, gensim, and the code from Bolukbasi and colleagues to allow the inputs back in, re-ran the original test set, and macro-accuracy dropped from 0.71 to 0.21 for the standard method and from 0.73 to 0.45 for the variant. The usual reason is that the second query term is returned when no close neighbour is found: man is to king as woman is to king.

So the computed vector's honest nearest neighbour is frequently one of the words you started with. The arithmetic moves you a little, and the exclusion rule does the rest. Linzen and Schluter had observed the same drop earlier, and the paper's own point is that although the constraint appears in the original work, it is not common knowledge and the examples are still widely quoted.

I would be careful not to overstate that in either direction. It does not mean the geometry is empty or that embeddings do not work — they are the basis of retrieval and they earn their place. It means the relations are weaker and noisier than the demonstration suggested, and part of the persuasion came from a filter.

The transferable lesson is the one I would actually use. When a result depends on excluding candidates, the filter is part of the result and belongs in the quote. Otherwise the number describes the system plus the filter, while the reader believes it describes the system.

problem.practice: Take any embedding model, compute the nearest neighbours of a computed vector — a relation applied to a new word — and this time do not remove the input words from the candidates. Look at what comes first. That is the result before the filter, and seeing it once permanently changes how you read a demonstration.

beats.broke: Comparing items by their surface form fails on every paraphrase, and enumerating meanings by hand covers only what somebody thought to enter.
beats.fix: Give every item a position in one learned space where similar contexts land near each other, so relatedness becomes a distance.
beats.cost: Distance measures what the training made nearby rather than truth or relevance, and the demonstration that made the idea famous depended on excluding the query words from the answers.

interview.q: What is a vector distance actually measuring, and what did the analogy demonstration exclude?
interview.trap: Treating closeness as evidence of a relation you have not checked. Two statements that contradict each other appear in near-identical contexts, so they sit close together — the space encodes usage, and usage is not agreement.
interview.answer:
It measures what the training objective made nearby, which is co-occurrence in the data the model saw. A small distance is evidence of similar usage — not of truth, not of relevance to my query, and not of any relation I have not tested. The case that burns people is contradiction, since two opposing statements occur in near-identical contexts and land close together.

On the demonstration: the 2013 paper reports that the vector for king, minus man, plus woman, is closest to queen, and it introduced a full test set rather than resting on that example. What the implementations do, though, is refuse to return the input terms of the query.

Nissim, van Noord and van der Goot allowed the inputs back into the candidate set in the standard implementation, in gensim, and in the code from Bolukbasi and colleagues, re-ran the original test set, and macro-accuracy fell from 0.71 to 0.21 for the standard method and 0.73 to 0.45 for the variant. The usual answer in the unconstrained setting is the second query term — man is to king as woman is to king — which is what you get when no close neighbour is found.

So the honest nearest neighbour is often a word you started from: the arithmetic moves you a little and the exclusion rule does the rest. Linzen and Schluter had reported the same drop earlier, and the authors' point is that the constraint, though present in the original work, is not common knowledge while the examples are still quoted.

I would not overstate it in either direction — embeddings work, and they are the basis of retrieval. The relations are simply weaker and noisier than the demonstration implied. The general lesson is the one I use: when a result depends on filtering candidates, the filter is part of the result, and quoting the number alone describes a different system from the one you have.

takeaway: An embedding turns relatedness into a distance, and the distance measures what the training made nearby rather than what is true — the famous king minus man plus woman result also depended on a rule forbidding the query words from being returned, and when they are allowed back the accuracy collapses, because the filter was part of the claim.
